nodes.question: What modernization efforts in Nigeria are linked to deforestation?
nodes.answer: Modernization efforts promoting full-sun cocoa in Nigeria are linked to deforestation.

nodes.question: What organization has promoted agroforestry practices in Nigeria?
nodes.answer: The federal-level Forest Research Institute of Nigeria (FRIN) has promoted agroforestry practices in Nigeria.
nodes.paragraph: 2020). In Nigeria, agroforestry practices have recently been promoted by the federal-level Forest Research Institute of Nigeria (FRIN)1 and in Ekiti State through the Forestry Commission (2021a). However, a return to traditional cocoa practices is likely to be complex given the country S previous push for full-sun modernization. For example, in Ghana, the reintroduction of oversimplified climate- smart agriculture (CSA) practices through private sector partnership has not sufficiently addressed issues such as a lack of tenure rights, potential rebound effects leading to deforestation, and agro- chemical dependence, resulting in some smallholder farmers being left with unequitable outcomes (Nasser et al. 2020). These swings in research and policy interests highlight the longstanding privileged role of external knowledge sources that have often deval- ued traditional knowledge and practice, only to later recognize their value when aligned with modern nar - ratives (Ajani et al. 2013; Makinde and Shorunke 2013). In Ekiti, there is a lack of understanding of how contradicting government policy dynamics for mod- ernization and sustainability interact with local knowledge and influence farmer decision-making for cocoa production on the ground.

nodes.question: What is the role of cocoa production in Ghana's economy and its impact on forest resources?
nodes.answer: Cocoa production accounts for approximately 4% of Ghana's national GDP and provides livelihoods for about six million people, or roughly 30% of the population; however, it has led to detrimental impacts on forest resources and land degradation, particularly in the cocoa forest landscapes.

However, recent economic growth, driven primarily by the cocoa industry, has had detrimental impacts on the country S forest resources and land degradation, particularly across the cocoa forest land- scapes in the High Forest Zone (HFZ) (Brobbey et al. 2020 ; Government of Ghana 2016 ; Nasser et al. 2020 ; Olwig et al. 2024 ). The HFZ, which is part of the West African Guinean Forest biodiversity hotspot, is distinguished by its dense tropical rainforests and abundant biodiversity, which arecritical for conservation strategies and carbon sequestration efforts associated with the global REDD +initiative (Car- odenuto 2019 ; FAO 2020 ; Nukpezah and Alemagi 2020 ). Ghana is also one of numerous sub-Saharan African coun- tries facing persistent challenges associated with highpoverty rates, especially in rural areas where the sustain- ability of livelihoods strongly depends on access to, and utilization of, natural resources (World Bank 2022 ). nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: Why is Ghana considered an excellent setting for a case study on REDD + implementation?
nodes.answer: Ghana is considered an excellent setting due to its abundant forest resources, high deforestation rate of 3.2% annually, and the heavy reliance of its economy and livelihoods on agriculture, particularly cocoa production.
nodes.paragraph: No Title Available DOI: DOI not available FullTextURL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s00267-024-02085-y Environmental Management (2025) 75:505 523 https://doi.org/10.1007/s00267-24-2085-y Exploring System Context Contributing to Emerging REDD + Collaborative Governance Regime in Ghana: Stakeholders Perceptions at the National Level Misharch Kwadwo Osei1 Received: 24 March 2024 / Accepted: 27 October 2024 / Published online: 21 November 2024 The Author(s) 2024 Abstract Since its emergence in 2007, the global mechanism for Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and Degradation in developing countries (REDD +) has raised hopes of providing cost-effective solutions to climate change. However, the design and implementation of REDD +projects in many developing countries, including Ghana, have faced complex governance challenges. In recent years, a collaborative governance approach has been increasingly recommended for effective REDD +implementation, but the impact of the dynamics of developing countries context on collaboration success remains unclear. Using Ghana S Cocoa Forest REDD +Programme (GCFRP) as a case study, this paper aims to increase our understanding of how the dynamics of developing countries context affect the drivers shaping the initiation of REDD + collaborative regimes for transforming cocoa forest landscapes.
